name: Parts of speech in Portuguese

ptBR.note: In Brazilian speech the small pronoun usually goes before the verb: Me chamo Ana. Portugal: Chamo-me Ana.

subtitle: Each word does a job in the sentence. Knowing the job helps you use the word: a noun has a gender, a verb changes for the person, an adjective matches its noun. Two Portuguese specials: prepositions join the article (de + o = do), and small pronouns join the verb with a hyphen (chamo-me).

concept.exampleHtml: A casa nova fica em Coimbra.

qa.html: Noun (nome or substantivo): names a person, thing or place: casa, médico, Lisboa. It has a gender. Article (artigo): comes before a noun: o, a, um, uma.
Verb (verbo): says what someone does or what something is: trabalho, comes, é. Its ending changes for the person.
Adjective (adjetivo): describes a noun and matches it: uma casa branca. Adverb (advérbio): says how, when or where, and does not change: bem, hoje, aqui, muito.
Pronoun (pronome): stands for a noun: eu, tu, ela. Preposition (preposição): a small word before a noun: em, a, de, com, para. Conjunction (conjunção): joins words or sentences: e, ou, mas, porque.
Prepositions join the article: de + o = do, em + a = na, a + o = ao, por + o = pelo. Moro na Rua Augusta. Venho do trabalho. do and na are a preposition and an article in one word.
Small object pronouns (me, te, o, a, lhe, se) usually go after the verb, with a hyphen: Chamo-me Ana. Vejo-o amanhã. After não they go before it: Não me chamo Ana.

concept.noteHtml: A quick test: can you put o or a in front of the word? Then it is probably a noun. Does it change with eu, tu, ele? Then it is a verb. Does it change with -o, -a next to a noun? Then it is probably an adjective. Common mistake: ✗ de o médico, em a casa → ✓ do médico, na casa. Next: Articles and contractions.
